section_1.title: Intuitive Hook: The Musical Note vs. The Drum Beat
section_1.content: Establish the prerequisite: The Fourier Transform decomposes a signal into its constituent frequencies. Introduce the trade-off: A pure, infinite sine wave provides perfect frequency information but zero time localization, while a short, sharp 'click' provides perfect time localization but spreads across all frequencies.
section_1.example: Visualize a long, smooth flute note (constant pitch) versus a sharp, sudden snap of fingers (no identifiable pitch).

section_2.title: Defining the Trade-off: Mathematical Visualization
section_2.content: Introduce the standard deviation (spread) in time (Δt) and frequency (Δω). Present the mathematical inequality: Δt * Δω ≥ 1/2. Use a visual 'container' analogy: if you squeeze the pulse in the time domain, it must bulge in the frequency domain to compensate.
section_2.example: An animation of a Gaussian pulse: as the bell curve narrows on the time-axis (horizontal), it automatically broadens on the frequency-axis (vertical).

section_3.title: Why Can't We Have Both? The Phase Interference
section_3.content: Explain that the Fourier Transform relies on global phase synchronization. To define a precise frequency, you need many cycles. If you truncate the signal (to locate it in time), you lose the phase information required to resolve the frequency, leading to spectral leakage.
section_3.example: A 'Chirp' signal (a frequency that slides) demonstrating that we can only measure frequency accurately if we allow the signal enough time to unfold.

section_4.title: Real-World Application: The Bat's Echolocation
section_4.content: Apply the concept to a biological context. Discuss how a bat must balance time resolution (to avoid hitting a tree) and frequency resolution (to distinguish between different types of insects). Explain that biological evolution optimizes this tradeoff.
section_4.example: A bat emitting a short 'click' to detect distance (high time precision) and a long 'frequency-modulated sweep' to identify prey texture (high frequency precision).

section_5.title: Summary & Reflection
section_5.content: Recap that this is a fundamental property of wave motion, not a limitation of our sensors. Conclude that the Uncertainty Principle is the 'tax' we pay when we try to observe the world through waves.
section_5.example: A final visual summary: a 'slider' on a digital dashboard that allows the student to adjust the width of a window, watching the spectral resolution degrade as temporal precision improves.

            "Define spread in time and frequency.",
            "Observe the inequality: delta t times delta omega.",
            "Squeeze time, and frequency spreads out.",
            "Gaussian pulses visualize this trade-off.",
            "Mathematical bounds are unavoidable."
        ])

        w_axis = Line(DOWN*1.5, UP*1.5, color=GREEN)
        
        # Gaussian curve representation

        freq_gauss = FunctionGraph(lambda w: np.exp(-w**2 * 0.2), x_range=[-4, 4], color=RED)

        self.place_in_area(VGroup(w_axis, freq_gauss), 'D1', 'F3', scale_factor=0.6)

        self.play(Create(t_axis), Create(w_axis))

        self.play(Create(time_gauss), Create(freq_gauss))

        freq_tracker = ValueTracker(0.2)

            .move_to(self.grid['B2']).scale(0.6)

            .move_to(self.grid['E2']).scale(0.6)
        ))
        
        self.play(time_tracker.animate.set_value(20), freq_tracker.animate.set_value(0.05), run_time=3)
        time_gauss.clear_updaters()
        freq_gauss.clear_updaters()

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 4 ===
        self.lecture[3].set_color(RED)
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 5 ===
        self.lecture[4].set_color(ORANGE)
        self.wait(1)
